n: *the promise of life*: See {{Romans 4:13-17|Romans 4:13–17}}. This letter to Timothy celebrates Christ’s resurrection and the life that comes from it ({{2 Timothy 2:8|2 Timothy 2:8}};{{2 Timothy 2:8|2 Timothy 2:8}}{{2 Timothy 1:10|1:10}}). The resurrection is the solution to the suffering and death of godly people ({{2 Timothy 3:12|3:12}}). Paul’s life demonstrates this hope ({{2 Timothy 4:17-18|4:17–18}}).

Paul and Timothy were very close friends. Paul loved Timothy like a son.

Paul prayed for Timothy every day and longed to see him again. Timothy had learnt about faith in God from his mother and grandmother.

He had received a gift of the Spirit when Paul placed hands on him. Paul wanted Timothy to use his gift faithfully to serve the church. He could do this by teaching the truth about Jesus.

Paul had taught Timothy how to teach the truth. The Holy Spirit would give him the power and love he needed to do it. The truth of the good news is that Christ has broken the power of death.

Upon Jesus’ return to earth he will judge all things on judgement day. He gives eternal life to those who trust in him.

Paul had been put in prison for spreading that message. Many people who had been Paul’s friends were ashamed that he was in prison. They deserted him when he was treated badly. But God’s Spirit gave Paul strength to face these troubles. The faith and friendship of believers like Onesiphorus and Timothy encouraged Paul.

- *as did my forefathers*: See {{Philippians 3:5|Philippians 3:5}}; compare {{Deuteronomy 6:4-9|Deuteronomy 6:4–9}}.

- *with a clear conscience*: This might relate to heresy (false teachings or practices) (see {{2 Timothy 2:17-18|2 Timothy 2:17–18}}; see also {{1 Timothy 1:5|1 Timothy 1:5}}). Or it could refer to Paul’s previous legal defense of himself (see {{Acts 23:1|Acts 23:1}}; {{Acts 24:14-16|24:14–16}}).
Giving thanks and prayer are common parts of Paul's letters (for example, {{Romans 1:8-12|Romans 1:8–12}}; {{Colossians 1:3-14|Colossians 1:3–14}}; contrast {{Galatians 1:6-10|Galatians 1:6–10}}).

- Paul urges Timothy to visit him (see study note on 1:5–14).

- *your tears*: Paul and Timothy may have last parted right before the Jews arrested Paul in Jerusalem and sent him to Rome (compare {{Acts 20:37-38|Acts 20:37–38}}; {{Acts 21:12-14|21:12–14}}).

- For information on Timothy’s family background, see {{Acts 16:1-3|Acts 16:1–3}} and {{1 Timothy 1:2|1 Timothy 1:2}}.

- *sincere faith:* Faith here means the Christian faith. However, Timothy’s Jewish heritage from his grandmother and mother shows his foundation in Old Testament teachings ({{2 Timothy 3:14-15|2 Timothy 3:14–15}}). Their Christian faith served as a model for him.

- Paul is gentle but firm in calling Timothy to come to Rome (see also {{2 Timothy 4:9|4:9}}, {{2 Timothy 4:21|21}}; compare {{1 Timothy 1:3-11|1 Timothy 1:3–11}}, {{1 Timothy 1:12-17|12–17}}). Suffering seemed certain if Timothy remained loyal. Paul wanted to strengthen Timothy’s determination.

- The mentions of the Holy Spirit in {{2 Timothy 1:6-7|2 Timothy 1:6–7}} and {{2 Timothy 1:14|1:14}} create an *inclusio* (literary framework) around this section.

- *fan into flame*: The Holy Spirit's work does not happen automatically. Timothy must cultivate this work with careful attention to his spiritual life (see {{Ephesians 5:18-21|Ephesians 5:18–21}}; {{1 Thessalonians 5:19-20|1 Thessalonians 5:19–20}}; compare {{Acts 4:31|Acts 4:31}}; {{Acts 7:55|7:55}}; {{Acts 13:9|13:9}}).

- *the gift*: This is the Holy Spirit empowering ministry (see {{1 Corinthians 12:1-14:40|1 Corinthians 12:1–14:40}}; compare {{Acts 6:3|Acts 6:3}}, {{Acts 6:5|5}}; {{Acts 11:24|11:24}}).

- *through the laying on of my hands*: Paul and the elders ordained (official ceremony of appointment) Timothy for ministry with a ceremony that included laying on of hands ({{1 Timothy 4:14|1 Timothy 4:14}}).

This verse summarizes the letter. Timothy would probably encounter suffering both when traveling to Rome and in his later ministry as Paul's follower ({{2 Timothy 2:3|2:3}}; {{2 Timothy 3:12|3:12}}; {{2 Timothy 4:5|4:5}}; see {{Hebrews 13:23|Hebrews 13:23}}).

- This passage emphasizes the importance of suffering for the sake of the gospel and encourages Timothy toward that end ({{2 Timothy 1:8|1:8}}; compare {{1 Timothy 1:15|1 Timothy 1:15}}; {{1 Timothy 2:5-6|2:5–6}}).

- *He has saved us … our Savior, Christ Jesus*: God and Christ are both described as Savior (see {{1 Timothy 1:1|1 Timothy 1:1}}; {{1 Timothy 2:3-4|2:3–4}}).

- *called us to a holy calling*: Salvation and godliness are connected (see {{1 Timothy 3:14-16|1 Timothy 3:14–16}}; {{1 Timothy 5:8|5:8}}; {{Titus 2:11-14|Titus 2:11–14}}; {{Titus 3:4-7|3:4–7}}; {{Ephesians 2:10|Ephesians 2:10}}).

- *and by the grace He granted us*: Grace is not given because we deserve it, but because God grants it (see {{Romans 3:23-24|Romans 3:23–24}}; {{Romans 5:6-11|5:6–11}}; {{Ephesians 2:8-9|Ephesians 2:8–9}}; {{Titus 3:5|Titus 3:5}}). 

- *by His own purpose … before time began*: See {{Titus 1:2|Titus 1:2}}; {{John 17:24|John 17:24}}; {{Ephesians 1:4|Ephesians 1:4}}, {{Ephesians 1:11|11}}; {{1 Peter 1:20|1 Peter 1:20}}; {{Revelation 13:8|Revelation 13:8}}. Salvation does not depend on human effort but only on God's grace.

- *he has revealed this grace*: The presence of God's grace is evident in history through Christ Jesus (see {{Romans 16:26|Romans 16:26}}; {{1 Peter 1:20|1 Peter 1:20}}).

- *through the appearing*: See study note on 1 Timothy 6:14. 

- *abolished death*: See {{1 Corinthians 15:26|1 Corinthians 15:26}}; {{2 Thessalonians 2:8|2 Thessalonians 2:8}}; {{Hebrews 2:14|Hebrews 2:14}}.

- *the way to life*: See {{2 Timothy 1:1|2 Timothy 1:1}}; {{1 Corinthians 15:53-54|1 Corinthians 15:53–54}}; {{Titus 1:2|Titus 1:2}}. 

- *through the gospel: Christ* provides salvation, but the proclaiming of the good news about Jesus is the way people receive his salvation (see {{Titus 1:2-3|Titus 1:2–3}}; {{Romans 1:16-17|Romans 1:16–17}}; {{Romans 10:14-15|10:14–15}}).

- Paul was confident as he encountered his own death (see {{2 Timothy 4:17-18|4:17–18}}; {{Romans 1:16|Romans 1:16}}; {{2 Corinthians 4:8-9|2 Corinthians 4:8–9}}; {{Philippians 1:20|Philippians 1:20}}). He set an example for Timothy to follow (see {{2 Timothy 1:8|2 Timothy 1:8}}).

- *what I have entrusted to Him* (or *what has been entrusted to me;* literally *my deposit*): The Greek phrase, my deposit, could mean either the good news about Jesus entrusted to Paul, or Paul’s life and ministry that he committed to God (see {{1 Timothy 6:20|1 Timothy 6:20}}).

Timothy must protect the important truth (literally *guard the good deposit;* see study notes on 1:12; 3:11). He is to do this by accurately proclaiming it and preventing false teachers from distorting it (see study note on 2:2; see also {{1 Timothy 6:20|1 Timothy 6:20}}).

- *everyone … has deserted me*: This happened either in Rome or in the province of Asia Minor when authorities arrested Paul. Paul might have considered this as another way his life followed Christ’s pattern (see {{Matthew 26:31|Matthew 26:31}}, {{Matthew 26:56|56}}). 

- *Phygelus and Hermogenes* are otherwise unknown. The context might imply that they were church leaders who sided with the opponents of Paul ({{2 Timothy 1:11-14|2 Timothy 1:11–14}}).
Paul encourages Timothy to remain loyal and to come to Rome without fear. He mentions both good and bad examples from others.

*You, therefore, my child*: In Greek, the word *therefore* connects this phrase to {{2 Timothy 1:15-18|1:15–18}}. The use of *you* as a directive emphasizes that Timothy's life should stand in contrast with the previous examples.

Timothy is again told to be strong and endure suffering with Paul ({{2 Timothy 2:1-7|2:1–7}}; see {{2 Timothy 1:8|1:8}}). Timothy should find motivation in the good news about Jesus and in Paul's example ({{2 Timothy 2:8-13|2:8–13}}).

Paul made it clear that Timothy needed God’s grace to follow Jesus faithfully. He also needed to work hard. The effort required was like the hard work done by soldiers, sports players and farmers.

Many people oppose the message about Jesus. Paul had been put in prison by people who wanted him to stop preaching it. Other people accept the message but argue about it. Fights about the faith lead people to stop believing what is true about Jesus. Paul mentioned two believers who had done that. He hoped that they would turn back to the truth.

Paul encouraged Timothy not to hold onto anger against people like that. Instead, he should continue to preach the truth gently. Timothy was a young man. Paul urged him to say no to evil things that tempt young people. Instead, he should do good works and be full of faith, love and peace.

Paul reminded Timothy of something important about God’s grace. Even when believers fail to follow Jesus faithfully, Jesus will always be faithful to them.

- *many witnesses: R*eliable witnesses would confirm the truth of Paul’s teaching (see also {{2 Timothy 3:10-11|3:10–11}}).

- *entrust these*: The verb entrust is related to the word *deposit* (see study notes on 1:12, 14). Timothy's task of guarding the deposit includes entrusting it to faithful men.
Paul quickly quotes a series of sayings about hard work, struggle, and reward.
Jesus Christ, descended from David, resurrected from the dead (see {{Romans 1:3-4|Romans 1:3–4}}). It's important to understand suffering with Christ from the point of view of future resurrection.

The apostle Paul’s suffering is an extension of the suffering of Jesus Christ. It emphasizes the crucifixion and resurrection as the core of the good news about Jesus ({{2 Timothy 1:12|1:12}}; see also {{2 Timothy 1:8|1:8}}). Paul’s suffering, like Christ’s, helped bring salvation to others. Christ approves of those who suffer and endure with him.

- *like a criminal*: Paul identified with the death of Jesus ({{2 Timothy 2:11|2:11}}; {{Philippians 3:10-11|Philippians 3:10–11}}). 

- *the word of God cannot be chained*: Both Paul and the good news about Jesus would be victorious through the power of Christ’s resurrection (see {{2 Timothy 4:17-18|2 Timothy 4:17–18}}; see also {{2 Corinthians 12:8-10|2 Corinthians 12:8–10}}; {{Philippians 1:12-14|Philippians 1:12–14}}).
*a trustworthy saying*: See study notes on 1 Timothy 1:15 and 2:5–6.

Timothy must focus on Paul's teaching and avoid the teachings and behavior of false teachers {{2 Timothy 2:8-13|2:8–13}}. The false teachings were probably similar to those in {{1 Timothy 6:20-21|1 Timothy 6:20–21}}.

*accurately handles the word of truth*: The Berean Standard Bible connects this verse to interpreting the gospel teachings correctly. Another possibility is that the apostle Timothy should remain focused on his teaching ministry and avoid getting involved in the arguments of false teachers (see {{1 Timothy 1:4|1 Timothy 1:4}}; {{2 Timothy 2:16|2 Timothy 2:16}}).

- Hymenaeus previously worked with Alexander ({{1 Timothy 1:20|1 Timothy 1:20}}). Both men continued to cause trouble through false teaching ({{2 Timothy 4:14-15|2 Timothy 4:14–15}}).

- Philetus became Hymenaeus's new teaching partner.

*They say that the resurrection has already occurred*: Compare {{2 Thessalonians 2:2|2 Thessalonians 2:2}}. These false teachers might have distorted Paul's teachings on resurrection ({{Romans 6:5|Romans 6:5}}; {{Galatians 2:20|Galatians 2:20}}; {{Ephesians 1:3|Ephesians 1:3}}; {{Ephesians 2:6|2:6}}; {{Ephesians 5:14|5:14}}; {{Colossians 2:12|Colossians 2:12}}; {{Colossians 3:1-4|3:1–4}}). They perhaps taught that people already fully participated in the life of heaven and that physical resurrection would not happen. They might have believed that a person's actions in the body did not matter because bodies that die cannot affect eternal spirits. 

Or perhaps they may have practiced extreme self-denial ({{1 Timothy 4:3|1 Timothy 4:3}}; see {{Colossians 2:8|Colossians 2:8}}, {{Colossians 2:16-23|16–23}}). They might have thought that enjoying material things was wrong for spiritual beings. These teachers might have interpreted the teachings of Jesus to mean he banned marriage ({{Matthew 19:10-12|Matthew 19:10–12}}; {{Matthew 22:30|22:30}}; {{1 Timothy 4:3|1 Timothy 4:3}}). Their perspectives on Old Testament law might have led them to promote certain things banned ({{1 Timothy 1:7-11|1 Timothy 1:7–11}}). They might have been too aggressive in promoting equality (see {{2 Timothy 3:6|2 Tim 3:6}}; compare {{Galatians 3:28|Galatians 3:28}}; {{1 Timothy 2:11-15|1 Timothy 2:11–15}}). 

They might have held to the belief that the future age had already arrived. Their teachings might have focused only on resurrection power, opposing Paul's message of suffering and Christ's crucifixion (see {{2 Timothy 1:8|2 Timothy 1:8}}, {{2 Timothy 1:12|12}}; {{2 Timothy 2:8-13|2:8–13}}; compare {{1 Corinthians 4:8-13|1 Corinthians 4:8–13}}; {{2 Corinthians 12:8-10|2 Corinthians 12:8–10}}). Paul describes their teachings as "irreverent, empty chatter" ({{2 Timothy 2:16|2 Timothy 2:16}}).

- Paul assures Timothy that false teachings will not succeed. He emphasizes the importance of being pure (see {{2 Timothy 3:9|3:9}}). 

- *firm foundation*: This metaphor emphasizes safety from destruction ({{Isaiah 28:16|Isaiah 28:16}}). It may suggest a temple (see also {{1 Timothy 3:15|1 Timothy 3:15}}; {{1 Corinthians 3:11|1 Corinthians 3:11}}; {{Ephesians 2:20|Ephesians 2:20}}; {{1 Peter 2:4-7|1 Peter 2:4–7}}; {{Revelation 21:14|Revelation 21:14}}). 

- *The Lord knows*: This quote refers to {{Numbers 16:5|Numbers 16:5}}.

- *"Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord must turn away from iniquity"*: See {{Isaiah 52:11|Isaiah 52:11}}; compare {{Numbers 16:26-27|Numbers 16:26–27}}; {{Leviticus 24:16|Leviticus 24:16}}; {{Psalm 6:8|Psalm 6:8}}.

Building on {{2 Timothy 2:19|2:19}}, the apostle Paul uses imagery of vessels in a wealthy home (see {{Romans 9:21|Romans 9:21}}). In God's household, Christians should strive to be like a valuable and useful vessel, not a cheap or useless one.

- *those who call on the Lord*: Compare {{Psalm 99:6|Psalm 99:6}}; {{Joel 2:32|Joel 2:32}}; {{Acts 2:21|Acts 2:21}}; {{Acts 9:14|9:14}}, {{Acts 9:21|21}}; {{Acts 22:16|22:16}}; {{Romans 10:12-13|Romans 10:12–13}}; {{1 Corinthians 1:2|1 Corinthians 1:2}}.

- *out of a pure heart*: See {{1 Timothy 1:5|1 Timothy 1:5}}.

- *a servant of the Lord*: See {{Titus 1:1|Titus 1:1}}; compare with {{Isaiah 42:1-2|Isaiah 42:1–2}}; {{Isaiah 50:6|50:6}}; {{Isaiah 53:7|53:7}}; {{Matthew 12:14-21|Matthew 12:14–21}}.

- *must be … able to teach, and forbearing*: See {{1 Timothy 3:2-3|1 Timothy 3:2–3}}; {{Titus 3:2|Titus 3:2}}.

*gently reprove*: Compare {{1 Corinthians 4:21|1 Corinthians 4:21}}; {{2 Corinthians 10:1|2 Corinthians 10:1}}; {{1 Thessalonians 5:14|1 Thessalonians 5:14}}; {{2 Thessalonians 3:14-15|2 Thessalonians 3:14–15}}; {{Titus 3:10-11|Titus 3:10–11}}; {{Jude 22-23|Jude 1:22–23}}.

Paul explains how people will behave in the last days, which had already started (see also {{1 Timothy 4:1-5|1 Timothy 4:1–5}}; {{2 Peter 2:1-22|2 Peter 2:1–22}}; {{2 Peter 3:3|3:3}}; {{Jude 18|Jude 1:18}}; {{2 Timothy 3:5|2 Timothy 3:5}}, {{2 Timothy 3:6-9|6–9}}).

In the last days people will treat each other badly. They will act the opposite of how Jesus taught human beings to live. They will follow their own desires instead of being controlled by God’s Spirit. They will teach lies about God. Certain people will try to trick others on purpose.

Timothy must stay away from people like that. Instead, he should follow Paul’s example. Paul was full of faith and love. He was patient and didn’t give up. He trusted in God to save him when he was treated badly. Timothy must also continue to be patient and careful as he taught about Jesus.

Paul called the good news about Jesus the Word. The message about Jesus is made clear in God’s word. Paul explained that God had breathed life into all Scripture. Breathing life into something is also what God did when he created human beings in Genesis 2:7. Paul meant that the Bible is more than a collection of words that humans wrote. God’s Spirit can use Scripture to teach believers and to heal wounds in their heart. Studying Scripture can train believers to do the good works God wants them to do.

Paul warned Timothy that he would be treated badly if he followed Jesus faithfully. People wouldn’t want to hear the message of truth. But he must keep doing the work God had given him.
Timothy must remain focused during the difficult times ahead.

*such as these*: These people rejected good teaching. They denied the power that could make them live as God desires ({{2 Timothy 3:2-4|3:2–4}}; see {{1 Timothy 1:5-11|1 Timothy 1:5–11}}; {{Colossians 2:16-23|Colossians 2:16–23}}).

The letters to Timothy and Titus consistently express concern about the impact of false teachers on households and women ({{Titus 1:11|Titus 1:11}}; see {{1 Timothy 2:11-15|1 Timothy 2:11–15}}; {{1 Timothy 3:4-5|3:4–5}}; {{1 Timothy 5:14-15|5:14–15}}). Whether or not these false teachers specifically targeted women, they were successful with some.
According to tradition, Jannes and Jambres are the names of the Egyptians who opposed Moses and practiced magic (see {{Exodus 7:8-13|Exodus 7:8–13}}; {{Exodus 8:18|8:18}}; {{Exodus 9:11|9:11}}).

- Timothy was from Lystra, near Antioch and Iconium, so he knew about Paul's suffering (see {{Acts 13:14|Acts 13:14}}, {{Acts 13:45-51|45–51}}; {{Acts 14:1-8|14:1–8}}, {{Acts 14:19-22|19–22}}). Paul recruited him after these events had happened ({{Acts 16:1-3|Acts 16:1–3}}). 

- *the Lord rescued me*: Paul could confirm from his own life that the Lord would fulfill his plans through his loyal servant (see {{2 Timothy 4:6-8|2 Timothy 4:6–8}}, {{2 Timothy 4:17-18|17–18}}; {{Psalm 22:19-22|Psalm 22:19–22}}; {{Psalm 34:19|34:19}}; {{Daniel 3:17-18|Daniel 3:17–18}}; {{2 Corinthians 1:8-10|2 Corinthians 1:8–10}}; {{2 Peter 2:7-9|2 Peter 2:7–9}}).

- From childhood, Timothy's Jewish grandmother and mother, Lois and Eunice, taught him the Old Testament Scriptures (see {{Acts 16:1-3|Acts 16:1–3}}; see {{2 Timothy 1:5|2 Timothy 1:5}}). Their lives reinforced their teachings.

- *the Holy Scriptures, which are able to make you wise … in Christ Jesus*: The Old Testament Scriptures give people the wisdom to receive Christ. At the same time, understanding Jesus Christ is necessary to fully understand the Old Testament Scriptures.

- *All Scripture is God-breathed*: This means it comes directly by God's own speech (see also {{Hebrews 4:12-13|Hebrews 4:12–13}}; {{2 Peter 1:20-21|2 Peter 1:20–21}}). This does not remove the role of human authors. It confirms that God is fully responsible for his word, and that scripture is true, reliable, and has authority. It is permanent and powerful because it comes from God. Its message is plain and consistent about Jesus Christ (see {{Luke 24:25-27|Luke 24:25–27}}, {{Luke 24:44|44}}; {{John 5:39-40|John 5:39–40}}; {{Acts 3:24|Acts 3:24}}; {{1 Corinthians 15:3-4|1 Corinthians 15:3–4}}). 

It has the power to bring salvation and inspire true faith. People must not abuse it, as some false teachers have done ({{2 Timothy 4:2-4|2 Timothy 4:2–4}}; {{1 Timothy 1:4-7|1 Timothy 1:4–7}}; compare {{2 Peter 3:16|2 Peter 3:16}}). But God's leaders must teach it correctly ({{2 Timothy 2:2|2 Timothy 2:2}}, {{2 Timothy 2:15|15}}). 

- As a result of its inspiration from God, all Scripture is useful. Both the Old Testament and the New Testament together guide and teach Christians in this life.

These verses expand on {{2 Timothy 3:15|3:15}} by explaining Scripture's effectiveness, its source, and how it provides wisdom for practicing the life of salvation. Paul was referring to the Old Testament. But his statement now applies to all Scripture, including the New Testament (see, for example, {{2 Peter 3:15-16|2 Peter 3:15–16}}).
Paul explains that salvation leads to living the way God desires ({{2 Timothy 3:15|3:15}}; see {{Galatians 1:4|Galatians 1:4}}; {{Galatians 5:16-26|5:16–26}}; {{Ephesians 2:8-10|Ephesians 2:8–10}}).

- *judge the living and the dead*: See {{Matthew 25:31-46|Matthew 25:31–46}}; {{Acts 10:42|Acts 10:42}}; {{Romans 14:7-12|Romans 14:7–12}}; {{Revelation 20:11-15|Revelation 20:11–15}}. 

- *His appearing*: See study note on 1 Timothy 6:14; see also {{2 Timothy 1:10|2 Timothy 1:10}}; {{2 Timothy 4:8|4:8}}; {{Titus 2:11-13|Titus 2:11–13}}; {{Titus 3:4|3:4}}.

Timothy's ministry truly existed in the presence of God and of Christ Jesus. Paul commanded him to work, expecting the return of Jesus to judge and establish his kingdom (see {{1 Timothy 5:21|1 Timothy 5:21}}; {{1 Timothy 6:13-14|6:13–14}}). 

Christ’s appearing will bring:

- spiritual cleaning ({{2 Timothy 2:19|2 Timothy 2:19}}),

- accountability ({{2 Timothy 3:8-9|3:8–9}}),

- salvation,

- declaration of righteousness, and

- reward ({{2 Timothy 4:8|4:8}}, {{2 Timothy 4:18|18}}). 

See also {{1 Corinthians 3:10-15|1 Corinthians 3:10–15}}; {{1 Corinthians 4:4-5|4:4–5}}; {{2 Corinthians 5:10|2 Corinthians 5:10}}.
This final statement summarizes the earlier points ({{2 Timothy 1:6-14|1:6–14}}; {{2 Timothy 2:1-15|2:1–15}}, {{2 Timothy 2:24-26|24–26}}; {{2 Timothy 3:12|3:12}}).
Paul gives some final leadership instructions and a testament to Timothy (compare {{Deuteronomy 31:7-8|Deuteronomy 31:7–8}}; {{Deuteronomy 34:9|34:9}}; {{2 Kings 2:1-18|2 Kings 2:1–18}}).

*being poured like a drink offering: *Paul regards his death as a sacrifice to God (see {{Exodus 29:40-41|Exodus 29:40–41}}; {{Leviticus 23:13|Leviticus 23:13}}; {{Numbers 28:7|Numbers 28:7}}; {{Philippians 2:17|Philippians 2:17}}). This offering participates in Christ’s own sacrifice (see {{Colossians 1:24|Colossians 1:24}}; see also {{Romans 12:1|Romans 12:1}}).
Paul's faithfulness, right standing with God, and reward are a model and a challenge to others (particularly Timothy) to follow Paul’s example after he is gone.

Paul believed that he was near the end of his life. He was like a soldier who had obeyed his officer and fought well. He was like a runner who had obeyed the rules and won the race. These were ways that Paul described how he had followed Jesus faithfully.

So God would reward him with the crown like runners received after a race. The crown or prize was that he would live for ever with Jesus. Paul longed for when that would happen.

While Paul was still alive on earth, he was suffering in prison. Many of his companions had left him. Paul didn’t have some of his important belongings. Through it all Paul was very aware of God’s presence with him. Paul described this as Jesus standing at his side. That is how near Jesus felt to Paul.

Paul suffered in his body. But he knew that he was safe in the kingdom of God.

Paul remained true to the trust (literally, "deposit") committed to him (see study notes on 1:12; 1 Timothy 6:20; compare {{Acts 20:24|Acts 20:24}}). He kept the integrity of the Christian faith and commanded Timothy to do the same (see {{2 Timothy 2:3-7|2 Timothy 2:3–7}}; {{1 Timothy 1:18|1 Timothy 1:18}}; {{1 Timothy 6:12|6:12}}; compare {{Romans 15:30-31|Romans 15:30–31}}; {{1 Corinthians 9:25-27|1 Corinthians 9:25–27}}; {{Hebrews 12:1|Hebrews 12:1}}; {{Jude 3|Jude 1:3}}).

- *crown of righteousness: *being declared righteous at the time of judgment was the only thing that remained for Paul (see also {{James 1:12|James 1:12}}; {{1 Peter 5:4|1 Peter 5:4}}; {{Revelation 2:10|Revelation 2:10}}; {{Revelation 3:11|3:11}}).

- If we live expecting that Christ will return, we will eagerly look forward to His appearing to establish his kingdom (see {{1 Timothy 6:14|1 Timothy 6:14}}; {{2 Timothy 4:1|2 Timothy 4:1}}). If we do not follow Christ’s commands, we will not welcome his appearing, because it will be as Judge.
Paul plainly commands Timothy to come to Rome (see {{2 Timothy 1:4|1:4}}).

- *Demas*: See {{Colossians 4:14|Colossians 4:14}}; {{Philemon 24|Philemon 1:24}}.

- *deserted*: Also see {{2 Timothy 4:16-17|2 Timothy 4:16–17}}; compare {{Psalm 22:1|Psalm 22:1}}; {{Mark 15:34|Mark 15:34}}. 

- *love of this world*: This contrasts with awaiting Christ’s glorious return ({{2 Timothy 4:8|2 Timothy 4:8}}).

- *Crescens* is otherwise unknown. The absence of Crescens and Titus seems to have increased Paul’s isolation.

- *Titus* was Paul’s effective and reliable fellow worker. He might have gone to Dalmatia (northwest of modern-day Greece) on a mission for Paul.

- *Luke: *The author of the Gospel of Luke and the book of Acts traveled with Paul at different times. Many believe Luke was Paul's physician ({{Colossians 4:14|Colossians 4:14}}). Luke was the only one of Paul's fellow workers who stayed with him continually. Therefore, Paul wanted Timothy to come quickly. 

- *Mark*: Paul's belief that Mark would be useful shows a Christian story of amending differences (see {{Acts 13:13|Acts 13:13}}; {{Acts 15:36-40|15:36–40}}; see also {{Colossians 4:10|Colossians 4:10}}; {{Philemon 24|Philemon 1:24}}).

*Tychicus* was apparently a Greek from Asia Minor (implied in {{Colossians 4:7-8|Colossians 4:7–8}}, {{Colossians 4:10-11|10–11}}); see also {{Acts 20:4|Acts 20:4}}; {{Ephesians 6:21-22|Ephesians 6:21–22}}; {{Colossians 4:7-8|Colossians 4:7–8}}; {{Titus 3:12|Titus 3:12}}). He was possibly going to Ephesus to deliver the letter and replace Timothy, assuming Timothy was in Ephesus.

- Paul's arrest and transfer to Rome apparently prevented him from gathering his possessions.

- *the cloak*: Winter was approaching ({{2 Timothy 4:21|4:21}}).

- *Carpus* might have hosted Paul in Troas. Mentioning Troas suggests Timothy was still in Ephesus and would travel through Troas, a port town.

- *my scrolls, especially the parchments*: These writings may have included Scriptures, personal notes, letters to Paul, copies of Paul's own letters, and other Christian and Jewish materials.

- *Alexander* was a common name (see {{Mark 15:21|Mark 15:21}}; {{Acts 4:6|Acts 4:6}}; {{Acts 19:33|19:33}}). Alexander the coppersmith was probably the same person mentioned in {{1 Timothy 1:20|1 Timothy 1:20}}. 

- *did great harm to me*: He probably did more than just oppose Paul's teaching. He might have been part of Paul's arrest.

- *At my first defense*: A Roman trial had two parts, a preliminary investigation and the main trial. Paul was probably talking about the first part. It might also refer to his first time in prison at Rome ({{Acts 28:1-31|Acts 28}}; see 2 Timothy Book Introduction, “Date of Writing”).

- *everyone deserted me*: See study note on 2 Timothy 4:10.

- *so that through me the message would be fully proclaimed:* Paul used his defense in court to share the good news about Jesus, similar to his past experiences ({{Acts 22:1-24:27|Acts 22:1–24:27}}; {{Acts 26:1-29|26:1–29}}; see also {{2 Timothy 2:9-10|2 Timothy 2:9–10}}; {{Philippians 1:12-14|Philippians 1:12–14}}). 

- *all the Gentiles would hear it*: Paul felt he had finished his mission ({{2 Timothy 4:7-8|2 Timothy 4:7–8}}). The Old Testament prophesies the conversion of nations (for example, {{Psalm 22:27-29|Psalm 22:27–29}}).

- *from the mouth of a lion*: The lion often symbolizes enemies (see {{Psalm 7:2|Psalms 7:2}}; {{Psalm 35:17|35:17}}; compare {{Daniel 6:1-28|Daniel 6}}; {{Hebrews 11:33|Hebrews 11:33}}). Here, it might mean: 

- literal lions in the Roman theaters,

- the emperor,

- false teachers, or

- Satan ({{1 Peter 5:8|1 Peter 5:8}}; compare {{Psalm 22:21|Psalm 22:21}}).

- God would continue to strengthen Paul and keep him strong in faith until the end of his life ({{2 Timothy 4:7|4:7}}; see {{2 Timothy 1:12|1:12}}).

- The Lord’s heavenly kingdom is different from this kingdom of earth that was about to judge Paul (see also {{2 Timothy 4:1|4:1}}; {{1 Corinthians 15:48-49|1 Corinthians 15:48–49}}; {{Hebrews 12:18-29|Hebrews 12:18–29}}).

- *glory … Amen*: Paul’s praise of God, even when facing death, shows his belief that God’s glory will remain (compare {{1 Timothy 1:17|1 Timothy 1:17}}; {{1 Timothy 6:15-16|6:15–16}}). 

- *to Him*: The Greek text implies this praise is for “the Lord” in the previous sentence, specifically referring to Jesus (compare {{Titus 2:13|Titus 2:13}}).

- *Prisca and Aquila *were probably in Ephesus at this time ({{Acts 18:26|Acts 18:26}}; {{1 Corinthians 16:19|1 Corinthians 16:19}}). They also lived in Rome, where Paul currently was ({{Acts 18:2|Acts 18:2}}; {{Romans 16:3|Romans 16:3}}). This suggests that Timothy might still be in Ephesus (see {{1 Timothy 1:3|1 Timothy 1:3}}).

- Paul is grateful when mentioning Onesiphorus in {{2 Timothy 1:16|2 Timothy 1:16}} for helping him while he was in prison.

Like in many of Paul's letters, this one ends with greetings and final instructions (for example, {{Romans 16:1-23|Romans 16:1–23}}; {{1 Corinthians 16:19-21|1 Corinthians 16:19–21}}; {{2 Corinthians 13:12|2 Corinthians 13:12}}).

- *Erastus* lived in Corinth ({{Acts 19:22|Acts 19:22}}; {{Romans 16:23|Romans 16:23}}). Modern archaeological digs found an inscription (carved writing) in Corinth mentioning an Erastus who was the city treasurer. He was probably the same man. 

- *Trophimus* was an Ephesian connected with Tychicus ({{Acts 20:4|Acts 20:4}}; {{Acts 21:29|21:29}}; {{2 Timothy 4:12|2 Timothy 4:12}}).

- *before winter*: Paul probably worried about a long delay if Timothy missed the chance to travel in the fall (see {{2 Timothy 1:4|1:4}}; {{2 Timothy 4:9|4:9}}). Winter weather interrupted travel across the Adriatic Sea from November to March (see {{Acts 27:12|Acts 27:12}}). Paul might also have been eager to receive his cloak for the cold prison ({{2 Timothy 4:13|2 Timothy 4:13}}). The New Testament does not mention Eubulus elsewhere. But he was obviously well-known to Timothy.

- *Pudens* was a name used by upper-class families.

- *Linus:* Both the bishop Eusebius and the bishop Irenaeus later identified Linus as the first bishop of Rome.

- The New Testament does not mention Claudia elsewhere.

- *brothers*: Greek *adelphoi*, a term for family members, both male and female.

- The unique phrasing here might emphasize what Paul already mentioned in {{2 Timothy 1:6-8|1:6–8}} and {{2 Timothy 2:1|2:1}} (compare {{Galatians 6:18|Galatians 6:18}}, {{Philippians 4:23|Philippians 4:23}}, and {{Philemon 25|Philemon 1:25}}).

- *with you all*: Paul intended that Timothy would read this letter in public.
